organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose collecting minimal labeled data and leveraging large language models like
GMT and T5 as the underlying dialogue engine. The system is then evaluated using
autonomous dialogue evaluation, and the results demonstrate its capability to
maintain designated roles while also significantly improving overall conversation
quality compared to existing models.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range, and its amplitude may be substantial enough to rival that of the gravitational wave background produced through binary tidal disruptions. Furthermore, SGWMB can be detected using detectors like LIGO and VIRGO, and its signals will exhibit a distinct'memory signature' that will often be obscured by noise, making the signal's detection and analysis even more complicated.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider; this framework predicts the universe underwent a phase transition around the time of the universe's birth that may create ripples in space time that scientists could detect. Developing a realistic model based on how this supersymmetry is broken, researchers found this phase transition can lead to a process that could explain an asymmetry in particle distribution, a phenomenon accompanied by additional ripples in space and possible black holes. These predictions can help clarify various particle puzzles and predict observations for follow-up studies.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility functions within an emergent communication language that is undefined at the start. At the physical layer, symbols from this language are transmitted, and the receiver utilizes the developed causal reasoning capabilities on received data to estimate the intended message. Experiments demonstrate that this semantic communication system enhances data efficiency and surpasses traditional schemes that rely on fixed signaling and knowledge about message causality.

The Natural Language Processing area has garnered disproportionate attention from researchers in the past. A primary factor driving this interest lies in the numerous practical applications Language Models can facilitate. This paper seeks to investigate a combination of Naive Bayes and Hidden Markov Models as a potential language model. By applying this model to a text, we can estimate missing words, taking into account the context in which they appear. We have derived the parameters for the model probability distribution functions, including those for Naive Bayes and Hidden Markov Models. To validate our model, we conducted a word prediction experiment using both the training and testing datasets. The results of this experiment emerge in the form of a table showing the accuracy of the predicted words for each given context. Better accuracy was achieved when the model was trained with more context information.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional methods. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM, which utilize Recurrent Neural Network and Matrix Factorization techniques, respectively. Both models process aggregated user session data but differ in their embedding approaches. STAMP converts item IDs into one-hot vectors, while NARM applies Rank-SVM for candidate rank embedding. Building on these successes, we introduce a Two-Stage Session-based Recommendation model incorporating fixed and moving windows. The proposed model leverages the strengths of both STAMP and NARM by implementing a two-stage recommendation process, where initial fixed-window candidates are generated through Matrix Factorization and subsequent moving-window refinement utilizing Recurrent Neural Network, all within a single framework enhancing state-of-the-art performance on public datasets.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to identify collective behavior and new phenomena that arise from the interaction between the dimer and activity gradients.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh of a fracture network, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-performance computing strategies. A mesh generation technique that handles problematic cases to maintain high mesh quality is provided. A versatile simulator utilizes process kernels to flexibly calculate fracture-friction, rock properties, and other phenomenon-specific attributes. The kernel method in this simulator enables the incorporation of various mechanisms without altering its underlying framework. A case study demonstrates the performance of this approach on an extreme scale, aided by high-performance computing facilities.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: first, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and second, designing methods to reassemble the disrupted formation efficiently (formation restoration). To address the first challenge, a new algorithm is introduced that leverages a cost-benefit analysis to assess the collision risk and energy required to reform the swarm formation. To solve the second problem, a previously developed point set registration technique is adapted for use with bead-based strategies, employing a centroid-based alignment approach instead of traditional feature detection and alignment methods that are often more computationally expensive. Use of this modified registration technique ensures faster formation restoration and enables swarms to recover from disruptions. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed algorithm results in lower energy expenditures compared to conventional registration strategies.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain the minimum Seidel energy for specific chain graphs of order $n$, along with presenting several unresolved questions.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking the self-adjoint Hill's equation for zero elliptic parameter. Our solutions, derived from the Lax-Deconick formulation, translate into quasi-periodic, non-self-adjoint Dirac operator eigenfunctions.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, this research utilizes stochastic geometry to develop an innovative analytical framework for the performance evaluation of vehicular networks incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile vehicle users. Our two-dimensional analytical model effectively considers the spatial interdependence of RSUs, vehicle relays, vehicle users, and road infrastructure using a Cox point process. By assuming relay backhaul to RSUs over reserved wireless channels and user association with the closest RSU or relay, we calculate the probability that a typical user is linked to either an RSU or a relay, determine the SIR coverage probability of a typical user, and subsequently, calculate the average effective transmission rate of a typical user within the network. This method enables the quantification of the increase in network performance resulting from the integration of vehicle relays in under-served areas.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to be an authoritative reference on various topics.  However, due to a limited number of editors and a vast amount of articles, only 0.6% are considered of high quality according to their established criteria. To enhance article quality through machine learning, we must first label individual sentences as high or low quality, yet this process relies on human annotations that are time-consuming and often yield inaccuracies. To resolve this, we developed an automated system that examines Wikipedia editing behaviors and assigns labels to sentences based on patterns related to article revisions. Our approach successfully generated labels for over 42 million sentences, matching the accuracy achieved by human editors in labeling 9,500 sentences as high or low quality. When compared to other automatic labeling methods, our system produced labels with comparable accuracy to those derived from human annotations for articles with available edit histories. Furthermore, we discovered that our labels can improve the performance of state-of-the-art neural network models that use edit histories to evaluate the quality of Wikipedia content.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is available, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the creation of a knowledge transfer matrix that can be used to train a distillation model through a zero-shot knowledge distillation process. When access to the original data is denied, the distillation model can be trained on a small set of query samples, which are obtained by actively sampling the data space and assigning soft labels to them based on their distance to the network's decision boundaries. This method demonstrates the ability to achieve accurate results on datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, with a model that wasn't trained on the original data.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is calculated to be 4.3$^{+0.5+0.3}$$\pm0.4$$\times 10^{-4}$, with the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction estimated at 2.8$^{+1.0+0.4}$$\pm0.5$$\times 10^{-4}$. The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode is found to be consistent with the predictions from the U-spin symmetry principle.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with ${\mathbb R}^n$ action, we establish a simple method for achieving this transformation. Our work rigorously addresses almost abelian solvmanifolds across arbitrary dimensions, offering clear group-theoretic criteria for classifying classical T-duals and resolving open problems from the literature in this domain. Furthermore, we successfully compute the classical T-duals of nilmanifolds, including nilpotent ones, through action of finitely generated abelian groups. Lastly, we show that the $C^*$-algebra framework unifies various definitions of T-duality from string theory by demonstrating a perfect equivalence between the $C^*$-algebraic notion and several definitions rooted in differential geometry and $K$-theory.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both useful and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less valuable knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple domains highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the effectiveness of inter-agent knowledge exchange in accelerating training.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the proposed metric function's reliability. Furthermore, we provide a method for determining the optimal bias in the metric function based on the code's lower bound. Additionally, we investigate and discuss alternative approaches to the PAC code family.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud-based hand joint tracking system, to estimate hand joint movement between frames. We also develop a net called HandShapeNet to estimate the 3D hand shape from the tracked joint positions. Both nets work efficiently on commodity graphics processing units. We create a large synthetic dataset with a vast variety of variations to train these nets, ensuring they can handle real-world data with ease. We evaluate our system on a large dataset called T-Hand, containing over 50,000 point cloud sequences captured in indoor and outdoor settings, and compare it with existing hand tracking and reconstruction methods on a set of 11,000 previously unseen poses, showing significant improvements in tracking and reconstruction performance. We observe that our system performs well even in difficult environments with large variations in hand pose, but further work is needed to refine it. This research is inspired by the challenge of automating industrial quality control, but the developed methods can also be applied in general purpose robotics and computer vision tasks involving human hands. The dataset and code are available for reproduction and further development.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring star, diamond, and saw patterns, using an odd prime number p and the field of p integers. We demonstrate that the reduced group remains a Coxeter group of rank 4 for all cases except when p ranges from 5 to 13. Additionally, the study provides information about the reduced group's properties using the field of p integers.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning in conjunction with a traditional calibration technique. The training process utilizes a vast dataset, 'BrAIVE', which comprises diverse real-world scenes captured by a depth sensor mounted on a robotic arm. The 'BrAIve-Kit' hardware setup allows for easy capture of scenes and facilitates the creation of a vast, publicly accessible dataset. The kit consists of a robotic arm equipped with a depth sensor and fiducial markers, utilized solely for setup purposes. A vast number of poses are automatically generated using an optimization method, and these poses are used to train a machine learning model. When operating in a real-world environment, our system employs this model to rapidly obtain initial pose estimates, which are then refined using a non-linear optimization process. The integration of our system's pose estimation capabilities into the 'BrAIve' framework allows for the seamless capture of depth sequences without the need for manual pose adjustment, a process previously feasible on desktop systems but not mobile ones. The system's accuracy, evaluated using various metrics including the'repeatability metric', compares favorably to established methods.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference in units, 
where the response is influenced solely by its treatment status and neighboring units within a defined radius of influence (K-neighborhood). Traditional approaches for identifying interference involve controlled randomized trials and statistical tests focused on specific, selected units (focal units). We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct a simulation to assess existing methods for detecting interference in networks. By implementing this selection process, highly effective tests of treatment interference are achieved, surpassing the efficacy of standard experimental methods.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are carried out. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and a star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can increase the standard model's predicted neutrino production by orders of magnitude. This process has the potential to exceed the standard model's predicted neutrino production by a star's core neutrino output.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the UNIONS/CFIS dataset utilizing ShapePipe, a cutting-edge pipeline. For comparison, we evaluated three different methods: ShapePipe, Ngmix, and MetaCAKE, to establish a reliable reference point. Our results demonstrate that ShapePipe accurately captures galaxy shapes with low noise and specializes in weak-lensing applications. Built upon the Jupyter framework, ShapePipe boasts an interactive approach, facilitating ease of use and customizability. Our analysis caters to a broad range of scientific objectives by providing multiple output formats and tailored data presentation options. To streamline data processing, we divided the UNIONS/CFIS map into 36 distinct quads, each consisting of roughly 480 square degrees. Our research utilizes these quads to produce a systematic map, showcasing ShapePipe's performance and noise levels. By combining our data with the KiDS 800-degree weak-lensing map for shear correlations, we confirmed that our results align with the predicted cosmological outcomes. Our research explores two distinct redshift bins based on photometric information and compares our findings with the KiDS 800-degree counterparts. Our analysis reveals notable agreement between our method and the one used in the Ki

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from the rotation sequence for no integer $m$, then, as $N$ approaches infinity, the parity of the sizes of sets consisting of numbers of the form $\{q\alpha\}$ within the interval $[0,b)$ that correspond to $q$ values up to $N$ displays evenly distributed occurrences.

The text also discusses how it answers a query put forth by Veech, thereby providing a revised mod $n$ form of a prior result (as stated in Theorem 4.1). A statement to the effect that the sizes of these sets remain uniformly thick, at a thickness defined in terms of $b$, for any given $N$ and $n$, and that they converge in probability to a certain probability, is a key finding that lays the groundwork for a number of other results including statements regarding the sizes of certain sets defined using a modified version of $\{q\alpha\}$, as well as a conjecture regarding the distribution of certain sequences related to $\{q\alpha\}$. We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We have observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, a moderate external magnetic field of around 3 Tesla is capable of triggering these correlations, which result in a measurable increase in the spin relaxation time. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of using a weak external magnetic field as a tool to investigate 2D BKT phases in materials with weak coupling.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a
u$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact the model. The likelihood of forming sterile neutrinos lighter than the Higgs mass is considerable, given the inflection point could facilitate their creation through a neutrino-axion interaction within the $a
u$MSM. The stability of the vacuum and consistency with dark matter observations in the $a
u$MSM rely on the requirement that these sterile neutrinos constitute all existing dark matter. The consideration of axion-particle interactions reveals that within this sterile neutrino dark matter scenario, the inflection point and narrow resonance axes could host additional, heavier states capable of being produced at lepton colliders through the $B$-mediated process. The production of these states could have implications for particle collider searches, given their potential to be observed within these facilities. The possible detection of these states at particle colliders presents further opportunities to validate the $a

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. Furthermore, the investigation yields refined bounds on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, ultimately leading to the creation of a strong simulation algorithm for circuits comprising Clifford gates and multiple instances of a fixed single-qubit Z-rotation gate, operating at a time complexity of $\text{poly}(n,m) 2^{m/2}$. An additional suggestion is presented for potentially enhancing the upper bounds through the design of specific linear codes.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours of observations to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances, metallicities, and extinctions. A good correlation was seen between the LAMOST and APOGEE study data. Furthermore, the LAMOST research team detected and validated around 460

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. However, such implementations often overlook the impact of fabrication process variations, which can compromise their randomness output. Moreover, existing examples of SRAM-based TRNGs are largely theoretical, and actual voltage levels required for sufficient entropy extraction often differ from proposed undervoltage values. To address these shortcomings, we introduced TuRaN, an SRAM-based TRNG designed for real-world applications. By exploring the relationship between bitflips and SRAM cell static undervoltage, we established a correlation that enables entropy extraction with high accuracy. Experimental results on two different FPGA platforms demonstrate that TuRaN maintains comparable performance while reducing power consumption, illustrating its capability to operate at lower supply voltages without compromising data integrity.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, making them free from spurious contributions. In this discussion, we explore the use of causal representation and box functions as a means to implement this duality. This framework allows for a straightforward evaluation of multi-loop amplitudes in regions where their causal form is typically within the domain of single-valued functions. Moreover, it provides a natural framework for merging all possible partial phase spaces, resulting in phase-space independent expressions that are still single-valued. While this framework is particularly effective for numerical phase-space sampling, it proves less suitable for phase-space integration. However, by combining it with techniques like loop-tree duality at one-loop and modern numerical integration methods, it is possible to achieve causal multi-loop amplitudes through a process called "pre-healing."

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done by Konno, et al. in the case of one-dimensional quantum walks with multiple states. Additionally, this paper confirms a specific set of eigenfunctions, similar to results found by Konno, et al. and Nakahara, et al.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-linear interactions, thereby yielding exceptional optical properties. Building on this idea, a study explored the optomechanical properties of a $q$-deformed cavity containing Fock states and a shifted rod, driven by an external laser. Notably, the study discovered that even slight deformations could produce amplified photon phenomena and that the system exhibited amplification, transparency, and negative refractive index. The application of $q$-deformation also facilitated observation of these effects at broader photon loss rates.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

To understand the origin of surface spin-orbit fluctuations in thin LaCoO$_3$ films, we investigate spin and orbital excitations using first-principles photon-echo calculations. We identify significant contributions from exchange, correlation, and anisotropy that influence the fluctuations. In LaCoO$_3$, we find that exchange and anisotropy dominate, whereas in LaMnO$_3$, exchange and correlation prevail. These results suggest that surface effects can modulate the relative importance of different mechanisms. We also demonstrate that surface relaxation, which is a product of film thickness and binding energy, can affect the fluctuations. This is particularly true for LaCoO$_3$, where changes in relaxation lead to varying contributions from exchange and anisotropy. Conversely, in LaMnO$_3$, the relative importance of exchange and correlation remains constant. These findings indicate that surface-controlled growth conditions can manipulate the weight of distinct mechanisms driving spin-orbit fluctuations in ultrathin oxide films.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for cases where the rate of random displacement slows with time. One of the most common methods for creating such systems involves leveraging dissipative optical lattices, and research has yielded numerous statistical results for Markov processes governing conservative motion. However, the literature lacks comprehensive information on the statistical characteristics of dissipative optical lattice systems. In this research, we provide a general framework for describing the conserved dynamics of particles in optical lattices, and our model is confirmed to be consistent with existing findings. We further analyze the momenta distributions of atoms in dissipative lattices, and our results indicate long-tailed non-Gaussian behavior. Moreover, we apply the phase-space thermodynamics concept to derive the phase-space density function of these atoms, thereby obtaining the phase-space density as a function of time in one and two-dimensional dissipative lattice systems.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate peaks in significant network connections during periods of high volatility, whereas the O-information findings reveal a rise in third-order relationships during times of heightened activity. Notably, leading cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin exhibit persistent network properties throughout the studied period.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for certain systems. The current research evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water using path integral molecular dynamics at the density functional theory level. Generally, the incorporation of zero-point motion results in more extended and less compact structures compared to classical behavior, thereby suggesting a reduced reactivity between components. Nonetheless, the impact of zero-point motion was found to be less pronounced when energy corrections are considered. The research indicates that zero-point motion has a notable effect on the properties of small clusters but its significance diminishes in larger systems.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. We establish that the compactification of a perception pair is itself a perception pair, and that the compactification of a space of group-invariant non-expansive operators is a minimal variational representation of the original space. We prove that the inner compactification of a perception pair is equivalent to the inner compactification of the space of its non-expansive operators. Additionally, when the group action is compact, we demonstrate that the compactification of a perception pair is a perception pair of measures on its compact quotient space. These findings are further illustrated through experiments in computer vision.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable gravity and quantum fluctuations. The results show that in both cases, the collective behavior of the quantum Hall state follows the same pattern, which is expected to hold true for other chiral systems as well. However, the violation of these relationships in the quantum fluctuation scenario might open the door to discovering new phases of quantum Hall systems via experimentation.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task due to the lack of a clear connection between their architecture and complexity properties. We identify and clarify this connection by developing a new concept called geometric complexity, which measures the complexity of a model's representation of its input space. We demonstrate that various forms of regularization, including those imposed by architecture and weight constraints, as well as dropout, effectively control geometric complexity. Furthermore, we show that the success of training deep learning models often relies on the combination of a suitable model architecture and an appropriate level of geometric complexity. We verify the efficacy of our findings through experiments on multiple benchmark datasets.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past studies have explored various methods of data augmentation in relation to automated essay grading.  In this research, we specifically examine the effect of different data augmentation strategies on transformer-based models, including BERT and RoBERTa, in the context of grading essay quality.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the classes of circulant toric models and Markov models, which are specific cases of marginal independence models. We explore the Markov projectivization of a graph's marginal independence model, discovering that it yields a perfect phylogeny when the underlying graph forms a tree. Through a series of statistical analysis examples, we highlight how the conventional toric model often fails to meet the criteria of independence, whereas the marginal independence model can accommodate this requirement.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of W boson production involving three massive gauge bosons at the LHC. Using a data set with 137 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity, they found W boson transverse momentum and rapidity in these events matched well with predictions from the standard model. Additionally, deviations from these predictions were not observed. A novel event characteristic - the W boson system's forward-outward orientation - was used to refine detection limits, resulting in a signal strength determination of 0.96 for the dominant three-boson production process, with uncertainties lower by about 30%. Also reported were constraints on anomalous W boson couplings, with deviations from standard model rates for certain processes seen at levels of up to 50 and 20 percent for signals involving charged leptons and neutrinos, respectively. With these findings, sensitivity to a mass threshold for a new heavy boson roughly twice the mass of a W boson was set at around 2.4 TeV for a particular scenario involving a particular type of anomalous coupling.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus.

We maintain that any subset $A$ of $\ell_p$, with $1\le p <\infty$, has an $\varepsilon$-isometric mapping from $A$ to $\ell_p(\mathcal{H})$, with $\mathcal{H}$ being a Hilbert space, such that for all $x,y\in A$, the relationship $\left\| \tilde f(x) - \tilde f(y) \right\|_p \ge \frac{\left\| x - y\right\|_p}{C}$ holds, with a constant $C$ dependent on $\varepsilon$, and that this mapping can be computed efficiently. We demonstrate that this result is nearly optimal by presenting an example of a sphere in $\ell_p$ for $p\ge 1\frac{1}{2}$, or $p=1$, which contains vectors $x$ and $y$ such that $\left\| x - y\right\|_p = 1$ yet $\left\| \tilde f(x) - \tilde f(y) \right\|_p \le \varepsilon \left\| x - y\right\|_p$, with $\varepsilon$ being arbitrarily small. Furthermore, we show that for incompressible subsets of $\ell_\infty$, a similar $\varepsilon$-isometric dimension reduction exists. We believe

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'learn' researchers' biases, raising concerns about the accuracy and safety of cooperative models. This study investigates how to address these concerns, focusing on cooperative modeling in solid mechanics.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance control systems with security features. This modular system works by incorporating an enhanced security assessment tool, which is based on an optimized control strategy that is informed by a security analysis algorithm. A specific security control strategy, which is informed by a data-driven security assessment tool, has been developed using a predictive monitoring system called System Level Synthesis (SLS). This specific security control strategy, which is informed by the SLS-based security assessment tool, utilizes an iterative algorithm that uses predictive models to optimize a security-related cost function. This optimized security control strategy, which is informed by the SLS-based security assessment tool, is then incorporated into a safety protocol to mitigate potential security threats. A specific safety protocol, which is based on an optimized control strategy that is informed by the SLS-based security assessment tool, has been demonstrated to effectively counter various potential security threats in an urban air mobility scenario.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the system's security breach can be guaranteed when the system's source intensity is lower than a specific threshold, thereby rendering the system insecure. Nevertheless, we propose a possible solution to enhance the system's security by varying the intensity of the weak decoy state.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the learned patterns, especially when it comes to semantic relationships. Secondly, a pretraining corpus of higher quality (as measured by expert assessments) enhances the model's in-context learning capacity. Thirdly, a pretraining corpus of greater size aids the model in acquiring basic knowledge, yet may impede its ability to learn context-sensitive information. Lastly, a pretraining corpus with domain diversity can improve the model's performance in areas outside of its pretraining domains, likely due to its ability to learn universal knowledge, albeit from diverse domains. Our findings provide initial insights into how a pretraining corpus influences the model's in-context learning capabilities, and we hope these insights will encourage the development of more systematic research in this area. Additionally, our research reveals a novel method for evaluating a pretraining corpus's quality using learning curves and reveals the benefits of a pretraining corpus with diverse domains that expand beyond its pretraining domains.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these formations quickly cool and detach while their cores take longer to respond, potentially leading to the creation of multiple, distinct shattering fragments. These fragments experience rapid expansion before becoming smoothly integrated into the surrounding hot atmosphere in a process aided by magnetic forces and convective mixing. Our findings also suggest that the growth of the central nebula is largely determined by a balance between cooling and the breaking and recombination of structures on smaller scales, while magnetic forces and convective mixing play a significant role in its formation and evolution. Conversely, thermal conduction has little effect until it is supplemented by other processes, at which point it begins to have a significant impact on the central nebula's formation.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions and as a sensitive indicator
for searching for signs of physics beyond the Standard Model. The discussion
starts with a review of the current knowledge of $C\!P$ violation in beauty and
charm hadrons, followed by a summary of recent results from the LHCb experiment.
The contributions then focus on recent findings from the LHCb concerning
$C\!P$ violation effects in beauty baryons and on the measurement of charge-asymmetry
in certain charm baryon decays. The topics discussed include the evaluation of
$C\!P$-violating effects in beauty and charm decays that are sensitive to the strong
interactions, as well as recent observations from the LHCb experiment concerning
the angular distributions in certain charm hadron decays. The contributions also
discuss the development of the flavour-tagging technique and its applications in
combination with the results from the simulation of the HL-LHC scenario. The
final part of this contribution presents the prospects for future investigations
at future collider facilities such as the High-Luminosity LHC and in potential
future colliders.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating energy-harvesting technologies into base stations, MNs can achieve sustainable operation without electricity costs. However, this requires specialized management to optimize resource allocation, balance energy supply and demand, and ensure network quality. Future MNs require intelligent management systems that can self-organize and adapt to changing conditions. This paper develops specific management procedures for energy management, resource allocation, and data traffic control to address the challenges of sustainable MNs. The proposed procedures leverage a data-driven approach, utilizing core network data and machine learning, to enhance energy efficiency and network performance. The procedures are designed to work independently and can be applied in scenarios with and without edge computing.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decays, and steady-state rhyme components, and are subsequently rearranged into acoustic units in an HMM-GMM framework. The USTIMES dataset was used to develop and evaluate the proposed approach, and the results show that the reconstructed transcripts using the identified acoustic units as a baseline perform better than previously proposed methods.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages within the subsequent optimization process. Through a detailed analysis on a quadruped robot and a comparison with existing methods, our proposed approach has achieved notable reductions in solution times and achieved 100% success rates where other methods faltered, particularly in navigating complex terrain with limited visibility.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By contrast, we have demonstrated that the metric plays a crucial role in assessing the relative utility of quantum states even in the context of unlimited resource availability, effectively serving as a necessary condition for achieving a physical transformation.
Consequently, our work has implications for understanding the relative accessibility of quantum states and has potentially significant practical implications in the realm of quantum information processing.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario without horizontal excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for steady solutions, whereas horizontal excitation led to resonance phenomena like increased occupation of the pendulum's phase space, primarily due to a resonant interaction between the pendulum's circular and linear vibrations. It was observed that horizontal excitation could cause motions previously considered stable to become unstable.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that DR-DSGD achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the performance gains of DR-DSGD over DSGD on various graph topologies, particularly when dealing with data class imbalance.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy states based on gluon occupation numbers, we derive a quantitative formula relating gluon characteristics to particle production. This formula is then verified using numerical simulations of energy states corresponding to various collision environments. The resulting calculations demonstrate agreement with experimentally measured data across a range of collision energies, diverse nuclear collisions and when analyzing the collision history via centrality thresholds.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means that less-strong magnetic fields are required to produce the high-velocity jets. For very high mass accumulation rates, the high-velocity jets appear initially, but quickly weaken and then disappear completely, which makes it impossible for these low-velocity outflows to form early in the protostar formation process, especially in magnetic clouds that are very weak, leading to different star formation processes than what is typically observed.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which ultimately enables comprehensive compensation and performance restoration. It is acknowledged that within a safety zone, certain thresholds can be tolerated for these destabilizing factors, prompting the need for corrective action only when the system's status poses a significant threat. Numerical simulation examples effectively demonstrate the proposed strategy's merits.

This research investigates the impact of solar pressure on artificial satellites in geostationary orbit, specifically exploring the phenomenon of resonance where a satellite's orbital period aligns with the Earth's rotational period or its half. The study identifies two types of resonances - first-order and second-order resonances, which arise from interactions with various elliptical orbits of the Sun and can cause saturating and unstable effects on satellite orbits. The analysis provides a method for estimating the influence of solar pressure on spherical satellites in resonance, citing various models. Numerical simulations validate the findings and offer insight into the behavior of spherical and prolate projectiles under solar pressure.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing TB models employs a non-relativistic framework which lacks a physically meaningful gauge invariance when approximated. However, when the approximations are eliminated and the smallest possible TB models are used, we show that the models become gauge invariant despite describing relativistic systems. We derive a condition which allows the models to remain gauge invariant when approximations are incorporated and demonstrate the procedure for relativistic KB approximations of semiconductors and van der Waals interfaces.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data with inherent ambiguity to identify objects within specific categories despite variations in appearance, pose, and shape. Picking up from previous PASCAL challenges, this study seeks to determine the most accurate object recognition approaches in the category-level framework. Our experiments reveal that PKNAP, a novel hybrid optimization algorithm combining pose, shape, and correspondence estimation, yields exceptionally robust results, particularly when dealing with noisy 2D keypoints. Our proposed method, PKNAP, demonstrates superior performance on the PASCAL dataset when compared to other pioneering techniques. Since practical applications often encounter noisy real-world data, we developed a robust version of PKNAP capable of effectively handling inaccurate 2D keypoints even without additional training parameters. Furthermore, our robust method proves adaptable to various PASCAL-derived datasets, such as PASCAL VOC, Kinect, and NUS-20S, with improved outcomes in object recognition compared to other competing approaches, highlighting its universal applicability and versatility.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups with pre-defined similarities, we find the minimum required trial sizes simultaneously. Our approach differs from conventional methods which rely on independent trials and ignores similarities within the data. We compare the new approach with conventional Bayesian methods that don't account for subgroup relationships. Both new and conventional methods perform well but the approach that considers subgroup relationships within the data performs better. We demonstrate through simulations that the approach optimizes sample size, achieving similar power to conventional Bayesian methods. Furthermore, the approach has practical applications in clinical trials, as illustrated by example protocols in treatment baskets for patients with specific disease characteristics and those with undifferentiated diseases and specific molecular profiles.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across varying views and objects, while its geometric representation is also transferable to classification tasks.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G result in infinite subgroups generated by a, b, and $\varphi(a)$. In this paper, we establish that various nilpotent quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $G_{n^2,p}$ possess the $R_\infty$ property. Specifically, we focus on subgroups $H_{n^2,p} \leq G_{n^2,p}$ given by nilpotent, torsion-free, non-Abelian quotients. Notably, we demonstrate that the $R_\infty$ property endures across various nilpotent varieties, such as hypercentric and metacyclic types. This research is closely related to prior investigations by Krasner, Campbell-Shalev, and Wladimirov.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case, 
our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step to reach this goal would be to thoroughly examine the stability of the Standard Model itself. We suggest that this can be accomplished through a combination of research at different types of particle colliders: high-energy accelerators, like the Future Circular Collider, to look for subtle deviations at high energies and smaller, lower-energy experiments, such as those at LHC with reduced energy, to look for signs of instability that may not have been found before.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and are consistent with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, this approach is capable of delivering reliable results even in the presence of noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for the vector kaon, providing confirmation of lattice QCD predictions; in contrast to expectations, we find a nearly symmetric longitudinal distribution and an obliquely shaped transverse one, indicating a substantial contribution to momentum from the strange quark.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. We identify necessary and sufficient conditions for the continuity of Toeplitz operators within these spaces, and establish the non-triviality of these spaces, provided that the condition on Fourier transforms is met.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to considerable domain shift variations. Traditional supervised learning approaches are unable to effectively address these challenges. We introduce an unsupervised learning approach, Cyclic Segmentation GAN, which combines CycleGAN and Segmentation GAN to perform domain adaptation and segmentation simultaneously from annotated images to unknown modalities. This novel method eliminates the need for manual labels on the unknown modality, instead using the supervisor's annotations on the source domain. Leveraging a segmentation generator, CSGAN iteratively refines unknown modality images and generates pseudo-labels for the training process. This approach was validated using MRI and CT images for multi-modal segmentation and compared to cutting-edge domain adaptation methods, demonstrating superior performance on datasets comprising diverse imaging modalities and medical segmentation tasks.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, is an RNN-based method for generating future actions that takes into account past observations and future contexts, using a key-value encoding scheme that can be applied to various action forecasting tasks.  By applying a radial basis function (RBF) kernel to translate raw data into a more informative feature space, the model's parameter count decreases dramatically, making it both efficient and effective.  We contrast our method with several prominent RNN-based models, including Simple RNN, GRU RNN, and LSTMs, and demonstrate its superior performance on standard benchmarks in both behavior cloning and offline action forecasting scenarios.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being extensively observed through high precision, long-term automated surveys. Yet, the physical processes responsible for these intense bursts of energy remain unclear. A renowned flare star, AD Leo, experienced a remarkable great flare on April 12, 1985, which provided scientists with notable data. Our analysis of the near-ultraviolet spectrum obtained during this flare offers valuable insights into the rapid chemical expansion of the stellar atmosphere. By modeling the observations, we identified an expanding photosphere with a radius of approximately 13 solar radii and a temperature range of 1.5 to 3.5 kilokelvin. Furthermore, our simulations reveal the presence of metal absorptions and a shift towards the red in the line positions, indicating rapid expansion. A temperature range of 500 to 3000 Kelvin is predicted for the stellar spots caused by the flare in the cooler phase, whereas these spots are expected to reach temperatures as high as 5000 Kelvin in the hotter phase.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, we examine p-core p'-partitions, which meet this criterion. Our analysis begins with feasibility proofs regarding the largest and smallest possible p-core p'-partitions. We then develop two distinct proofs to determine the probability distribution of a specific partition type within the set of all p-core p'-partitions. One proof utilizes lattice paths and the mirror symmetry of these paths, while the other draws from the concept of walks on a graph with a finite residue field. We also make a connection between the largest p-core p'-partitions and a type of combinatorial identity known as Glaisher's conjecture.
