Additionally, we deduce information about the maximum and minimum possible values of the third largest partition element in the set of all p-core p'-partitions.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains, but their reliance on synthetic data poses challenges due to the difficulties of creating such data and ensuring its accuracy. Existing synthetic data generation methods often fail to replicate real-world point clouds precisely, which can harm the models' performance and lead to hazardous mispredictions. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel framework called Transformation-pecific Point Cloud (TPC) smoothing, aimed at improving the accuracy of the models by addressing the inherent flaws of synthetic data generation. The proposed TPC smoothing method leverages transformation-specific smoothing functions, applied to the point clouds, which effectively corrects geometric distortions and enhances the models' robustness across various scenarios. The method's versatility allows it to be applied at different stages: both during training on a small synthetic dataset and fine-tuning on real-world data. Evaluation metrics demonstrate that TPC smoothing enhances the models' synthetic data training accuracy and real-world robustness, representing a groundbreaking contribution to the field.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave radar networks with a focus on modifying established protocols to meet the unique requirements of radar systems. Our analysis begins by examining ALOHA and CSMA, the basic protocols most wireless systems utilize. We introduce a slotted ALOHA variant, allowing radar nodes to transmit on designated time slots while other slots remain available. Our work also extends CSMA, enabling nodes to transmit only during assigned frames and penalizing transmission errors with a longer waiting period. Our findings reveal that while CSMA outperforms the modified slotted ALOHA under most network conditions, it falters in high-load scenarios. Our proposed CSMA variant surpasses the standard CSMA under all circumstances. Moreover, our research highlights that both access methods function as pure ALOHA at low load levels. Our results show that CSMA and the modified slotted ALOHA achieve comparable throughputs at high load levels. To validate our analytical findings, we conduct simulations utilizing the Simulink software.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. A new investigation adopts a distinct approach, focusing on analyzing changes in a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferogram resulting from entangled photon interaction. Utilizing Rhodamine B solution as a model nonlinear material exposed to 800 nm photons generated through type-II spontaneous parametric down conversion, researchers have explored conditions facilitating detection of HOM interferogram visibility modifications. A supporting model incorporates a spectral perspective to elucidate observed changes in the HOM interferogram, revealing that visibility reductions can be quantified based on specific absorption coefficients and photon pair energies. These findings contribute to a deeper comprehension of entangled two-photon absorption and its manifestation in Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of low-rank tensor
decomposition that employs a dual time-aware representation of temporal knowledge
graphs. We recognize that existing temporal knowledge graph models often
overlook the one-to-many problem, where a single knowledge node can relate to
multiple time periods. We address this issue by introducing a dual time-aware
representation, where each temporal knowledge graph can be represented by two
matrices that capture one-to-many and one-to-one relationships, respectively.
Furthermore, we develop a temporal unifying framework that unifies various knowledge
graph models and enables transfer learning, and introduce several strategies to
enhance its performance. We evaluate our method along with six other state-of-the-art
approaches on multiple datasets, revealing that our approach outperforms existing
models in accurate inference and hyperparameter optimization.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at an optimal angle.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant attention. Previous research has mainly focused on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs, whereas we shift the focus to "sometimes-type" proofs and enhance it by showing that the correlations used can be of lower than perfect accuracy, which has positive implications for experimental practices. Additionally, we highlight that "sometimes-type" proofs are more versatile than "always-type" proofs by indicating how they can be naturally extended to yield higher certainty in scenarios with multiple outcomes, an area of study previously dominated by inequalities. This research aims to contribute to the understanding of Bell nonlocality and its applications in quantum physics and philosophy.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems with an imbalance in sublattices fall into this category. Following a general description of constructing flat bands through MOs, various examples are examined with numerical proof, including the sawtooth lattice in one dimension and the hyper-Pyrochlore lattice across any number of dimensions.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Furthermore, van Hove singularities in the density of states contribute to the instability of the normal state, highlighting the need for further correction through accounting for van der Waals effects. Given its simplistic monolayer form, hydrogen boride can serve as a valuable test subject for exploring superconducting properties in extremely low-dimensional systems.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve. The findings presented here coincidentally relate to the count of partitions where each part's size is a multiple of a specific number and, when the partition is flattened, the resulting sequence does not contain the number zero. The proof of a combinatorial identity mentioned here interestingly connects to the concept of run counting in permutations' FLAP framework.

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study a group's behaviour under recurring symmetries and explore its internal structures, establishing a relationship between recurring symmetries and a group's stable components, and derive a classification system for these internal structures. Additionally, we investigate a group's behaviour under specific transformations and its impact on patterns and characteristics, understanding a group's movement and its effect on patterns and characteristics when a particular element has a significant impact.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To ensure system safety and effectiveness, our work focuses on verifying and validating a fail-operational autonomous driving system through formal verification. Building on a core model of controlled vehicle movement, we have formally established and proven the significance of fail-safe automated driving under assumptions rooted in real-world conditions. By leveraging a toolset incorporating predicate abstraction and SMT solving, our modeling efforts translate fail-safe behaviors into reversible transitions, encompassing both driving modes and vehicle movements. Furthermore, we have incorporated a strategy for generating fail-safe states via an optimized path-rearrangement technique, allowing for finite verification of complex fail-safe conditions. Through case-specific modeling, our methodology has successfully passed industrial-style verification as part of an FMCAD 2020 competition.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has focused on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  This article examines three specific frameworks - a real numbers-based approach, a formalism emphasizing bound variables, and a system incorporating infinitesimal quantities - all of which provide unique insights into Leibnizian calculus.  By analyzing the operations of differentiation and integration within these frameworks, as well as discussing their applications to specific problems, this article aims to demonstrate the versatility of Leibnizian calculus, showing it to be capable of efficiently handling a diverse set of computational tasks.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most relevant parameters are the cold dark matter density, the Hubble constant, the primordial power spectrum amplitude and the linear HI bias. When assuming that foregrounds can be effectively removed, we find that we can achieve a similar accuracy as with a model that perfectly represents the power spectrum, which is the assumed case for the noise-corrected model. The accuracy that we achieve is comparable to what is expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys, which shows that HI intensity mapping can be a powerful tool for determining cosmological parameters if it is combined with other data. When including the effects of foregrounds that remain after being removed using

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence spaces isomorphically into another sequence space, then T's image contains an infinite-dimensional subspace. In this research, we diverge from their line of inquiry but still explore how a linear operator's image dimensionality relates to the dimensionality of its domain. Our key discovery is that there exists no single linear operator capable of mapping any infinite-dimensional space onto a finite-dimensional space while maintaining a direct relationship. This finding supplements Hasannasab and Zabihyan's previous findings and offers a sharper contrast to Christensen and Hasannasab's previous result.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary data sources. Nonetheless, incorporating additional data may lead to increased complexity and potential harm via data privacy breaches. This research presents a basic framework for a hybrid recommender system that integrates content-based and behavior-based methods with an emphasis on utilizing supplementary data sources effectively. A content-based method leveraging document context (i.e., topics) learned from latent topic models is incorporated to mitigate data scarcity. Conversely, a behavior-based method, which utilizes user-item interaction data with an emphasis on temporal dynamics, is employed to account for users' and items' evolving temporaal patterns. This hybrid model is compared to standard content-based and behavior-based methods through experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating improved performance and greater flexibility when supplemented by data source expertise.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already present at $O(N^{-1})$. A specific form of type $B$ freeness, denoted as $\text{type } B_1$, is shown to appear at $O(N^{-1})$. $\text{type } B_1$ freeness implies the asymptotic linearization of noncentral quadratic statistics.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on the contribution
from the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ mixing as well as from the rescattering of
amplitudes. Our investigation shows that the final state contains several components
including $s\bar s$ molecular states, $q\bar q$ components and the physically
nonzero elements of the $a_0(980)$ amplitude. Utilizing the isospin symmetry,
the branching ratio $\mathcal B(\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980))$ is related to
$\mathcal B(a_0(980) \to \pi^+\pi^-)$. Furthermore, the contribution from the
$f_0(980)-a_0(980)$ mixing in the decay process is found to be unimportant. 
Our final calculation yields the branching ratios $\mathcal B(\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
f_0(980)) = (3.8 \pm 1.1) \times 10^{-4}$ and $\mathcal B(\bar B_s^0 \to
J/\psi a_0(980))$.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical components to redirect a substantial portion of the MMT's light towards the GSEF instrument during operational observations, and also facilitates separate science observations of the telescope's aperture during non-GRAVITY scheduled time. The camera's optical elements effectively increase the MMMT's overall gain by approximately two orders of magnitude for wavelengths ranging from 1.5 to 2.2 micrometers. The GraQuAC camera's optical performance has been thoroughly evaluated using various optical tests which revealed that its optical train maintains an accuracy of less than 1% over the MMMT's 140 x 8.2 arcsecond field of view. The GraQuAC camera was then transported to the MMMT in July 2016 for on-sky optical assessments which involved measuring its half-plane modulation level, also known as the Panschke effect, which is instrumental in determining the MMMT's relative aperture gain. It is worth mentioning that a significant objective of these on-sky tests was to verify that the GraQuAC camera wouldn't generate any observable light loss or loss of MMMT's parallax view during GRAVITY or independent MMMT observations.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters on doubling metric spaces. Conversely, for the more constrained highway dimension space, we prove that no such scheme exists, and this distinction applies to a broader family of issues, including Capacitated $k$-Center, k-Means, and Steiner $k$-Center issues.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the linear system as well as the error rate. As part of an ongoing series on solving polynomial linear systems with errors, we build on our previous findings, including a proof from [Guerrini et al., Proc. ISIT'19], that a lower bound on evaluations can be achieved when errors are randomly distributed, even for large error rates. This paper makes two significant contributions. Firstly, it proves a new evaluation bound for random errors with an improved accuracy, surpassing our previous result from [Couvreur et al., Proc. CURVE'20]. Secondly, it introduces an early termination technique for extracting interpolation moduli in finite fields to recover the solution, providing an improved accuracy over our previous result from [Guerrini et al., Proc. CURVE'20]. This technique also has a reduced computational cost. Both the new bound and the early termination technique are versatile and applicable to various coding theories, including Reed-Solomon codes and Castryck-Fletcher-Moussese codes.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon production. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking states with various chiral imbalances are explored. By utilizing a finite fermion molecular gas approach, the spectral density of TMD correlator for vector mesons is determined. A medium with local parity breaking and chiral imbalance is induced by a fermion molecular gas at finite temperature and chemical potential. Our findings reveal that local parity breaking significantly impacts the transverse polarization of vector mesons in the presence of chiral imbalance. Moreover, the longitudinal polarization of vector mesons exhibits sensitivity to the mass of vector mesons.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of log(n), by gathering short, altered path lengths from specific nodes, averaging these lengths, and applying a pre-defined protocol to determine the network's size. Our study also involves evaluating how vulnerable networks are to attacks involving fake node creation and how difficult it is to detect such attacks.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy yields multiple solutions for the metric variables, which are distinguished by distinct mean curvatures. We demonstrate the method's applicability with newly constructed initial data sets for a gravitating ring and a rotating ring larboard.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector surrounded by photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which necessitated a thorough assessment of the PMTs. Over four years, starting from 2017, a rigorous testing program for nearly 20,000 20-inch PMTs was carried out by the JUNO team. By examining these PMTs and implementing a series of stringent requirements, the experiment's investigators were able to verify the high quality of the selected instruments. This study outlines the thorough testing procedures used, the stringent standards for the experiment's PMTs, and the results of the 20-inch PMTs tested. It also reviews the technological advancements that led to the improved quality of these instruments.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable. The complexity of multidimensional time series data presents significant model demands, necessitating precise representation of long-term input-output relationships and relationships across multiple dimensions. Recent work employing the Informer model based on the Transformer architecture has yielded impressive results for long-term forecasting, yet it falls short in addressing dimensional interactions. Our proposed dimension-adaptive Informer framework, known as DAM, overcomes this limitation by incorporating a novel adaptive attention mechanism that incorporates dimensionality awareness. This breakthrough enables the model to capture valuable spatial dependencies within forecasting tasks. Our proposed framework incorporates an innovative regression component that enhances low-frequency signal forecasting. Our extensive experiments reveal that DAM surpasses state-of-the-art results for multivariate and TVP-LSTF challenges on the M4 dataset, and also establishes a new benchmark for the real-world energy forecasting challenge in the NEU-ENERGY dataset.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of ADCs for the future.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label information within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because low-frequency fluctuations will occur as well due to its wave-like properties. A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually be searching for much larger and unexplored ranges of frequencies. A network of sensors, by cross-correlating their measurements, can detect these low-frequency fluctuations, and is not limited by bandwidth because low-frequency fluctuations will occur simultaneously at a range of frequencies. In this way, existing sensor networks can be used to experimentally explore the unexplored ranges of the parameter space of this bosonic dark matter.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, and hence its uniqueness or lack thereof, is established based on the conditions under which a certain matrix's null space has a nonempty dimension. The study further analyzes the stability of the solution to BPC and determines the optimal recovery order of the method in terms of the number of Fourier degrees of freedom, with a variant of BPC exhibiting nearly optimal recovery order in certain cases.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with a comprehensive implementation available through the V1 model and PISCES toolset. However, commercial hardware vendors like Mellanox and Intel have introduced their own proprietary switches and compilers, each with distinct programming interfaces and features tailored to the specifics of the underlying hardware. The Mellanox A4000 switch, for instance, requires the MELL compiler to compile P4 programs into table configurations, utilizing a hardware-specific programming interface. Our research utilizes open-source software to develop an P4 compiler backend for configuring the A4000 and Sc2000 switches, leveraging a generic and vendor-agnostic framework to maximize flexibility and ease of use.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. However, the standard finite element methods that use the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements in two and three dimensions suffer from inaccurate representations of some transport equations. This inaccuracy arises because the spatial discretisation is not sufficiently precise. This paper presents schemes to enhance the accuracy of transporting scalar, vector, and tensor fields across curved surfaces in two and three dimensions. We apply these schemes to transport equations involving curl and divergence operators, and demonstrate that they yield significantly improved results. Furthermore, we validate the performance of these schemes in numerical experiments against exact solutions.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, German credit, and Bank data sets demonstrate that by combining all three methods, it is possible to attain highly accurate predictions, while guaranteeing fairness and maintain users' data confidentiality.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method shows promising results on various image classification and sequence prediction tasks with significant performance enhancements.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Consequently, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit increased stability when subjected to low levels of dissipation.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window where the mass difference between two lepton types lies between their sum and the absolute difference. Although a moderately large interaction between this scalar field and the two lepton types could lead to extended lifetimes and larger observable distances between their birth and death points. By leveraging existing neutrino experiments and an upcoming one, we plan to explore various possible scenarios of this theoretical model. For instance, we can utilize data from the muonium decay rate and LSND production and decay patterns to evaluate this scalar's coupling, excluding the mass window indicated by the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly in the electron-muon sector. Furthermore, we analyze three major production processes of these scalar particles at beam dump experiments, such as the Drell-Yan process, heavy meson decay, and muon scattering, to derive constraints from the CHARM and NuTeV experiments and gauge the detection capabilities of the upcoming SHiP beam dump experiment which has the ability to exhaustively explore the mass window linked to the muon anomalous magnetic moment anomaly.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different charge.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures. We establish that any solution with bounded variation for this system is not only unique but also constitutes a weak solution, which, due to the lack of differentiability, cannot be expressed as a usual solution involving functions. As a result, we investigate the existence of solutions with bounded variation and, by restricting the initial data to certain subsets of states, demonstrate the existence of solutions with bounded variation for the full measure. Conversely, we show that, under certain conditions, a weak solution with bounded measure can be obtained when the initial data include only those states.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices with IoT or industrial applications. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three Naive Bayes variants are explored, including the original Naive Bayes, Naive Bayes with feature selection, and Naive Bayes and feature selection coupled with data pruning. The latter two approaches significantly outperform the original Naive Bayes in accuracy and computational resource efficiency. Furthermore, three network datasets are utilized to demonstrate the versatility of NBcoded in various network attack detection scenarios, including DNS, TCP, and mixed traffic. In addition to outperforming existing low-resource classifiers in accuracy, NBcoded also effectively reduces resource requirements on devices without sacrificing accuracy.

For finitely generated groups, we establish a growth condition based on action. If a group can be decomposed into virtually abelian subgroups with combined index bounded by $n^r$, then its action-induced growth function attains a certain exponent, namely $\max\{1 + \frac{\log n}{\log k}, r\}$, where $k$ represents the largest factorial coefficient in the group's growth function. Our work is exemplified by several classes of solvable groups, including metabelian groups with distinct growth properties and a metabelian group exhibiting divergent stable growth.

Animals move in various ways, utilizing distinct locomotion patterns that
can be analyzed through visual observations. This paper proposes a computational
method for identifying the movement of animals, distinguishing between different
types of movement, and detecting the body parts involved in the movement, all
from video footage. The research acknowledges that identifying biological motion
in videos can have several animal conservation applications and has made
preliminary findings in this area. Though the research has made progress in this
area, there is still much to be explored and several complex problems to be
addressed. The researchers are looking to collaborate with biologists and other
experts in animal behavior to further develop this field.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be a difficult task. Our research highlights two major obstacles: the need to recognize ambiguities inherent to the law and the challenges associated with inferring a physical law that may contradict existing knowledge. To address these limitations, we suggest introducing uncertainties into the modeling process and propose a new metric that assesses the relevance of new data to established physics. The proposed framework effectively captures the essence of physics, allowing for the discovery of physics principles and governing equations even in complex systems with multiple interacting components. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of this approach by successfully uncovering previously unknown physical interactions between fluids and obstacles, as well as the dynamics of bouncing balls, which often defy physical intuition.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits increased by 220 GeV, 360 GeV and 380 GeV respectively for certain specific scenarios and models.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38. We achieved a high Purcell factor with only mild enhancements to the nanobeam's and the underlying substrate's adiabatic modifications. This optimized design features a nanobeam with a 3 μm gap between the nanobeam and an integrated feeder waveguide, as well as a unique feeder waveguide design. Furthermore, we collected single-photon data from the optimized source, demonstrating a high extraction efficiency of 93 percent and a respectable photon collection efficiency of 95 percent for our on-chip single-photon source.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak. The work presents an in-depth examination of the boson peak's characteristics in three substances with varying excitation energies. By analyzing the intensity and wavevector dependence of the boson peak, we can determine the system's volume and constraints. Furthermore, the study reveals that the excitation energy of the boson peak is directly related to the vibrational state in the ground state, as well as anisotropic motion within it.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods like sector decomposition and 
are then translated into physical scenarios with a series solution, providing 
precision up to fifth derivatives. This method has an overall accuracy of 
10^-8 and is used to solve examples in quantum electrodynamics and scalar 
quantum mechanics.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types.

Researchers have identified a previously unknown spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which stretches across 3 kiloparsecs in radius. This arm contains star-forming regions and young massive stars, aged approximately 13 million years. The newly detected arm passes close to the Central Molecular Zone, a dense molecular cloud that overlaps with the galactic center. The presence of young stars in this area suggests they were formed locally. The discovery of the far 3-Kpc arm reduces the likelihood of it being an extension of a more distant spiral arm, thought to be a separate entity called the far side of the Central Molecular Zone. In contrast, a study modeling the galactic spiral arms provides further evidence for its existence. In particular, a feature appearing in a galactic map, derived from 2MASS star counts, aligns with the far 3-Kpc arm. This was confirmed by eliminating neighboring features through a cross-validation method.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison across multi-objective optimization, multimodal optimization, and quality diversity in a straightforward context reveals that multi-objective optimization may not consistently generate significant diversity. By contrast, multimodal optimization tends to yield solutions with superior fitness levels. Meanwhile, quality diversity proves to be resilient to genetic neutrality and yields the most diverse set of solutions overall. Furthermore, integrating an autoencoder allows for the automated discovery of phenotypic features, which, in conjunction with quality diversity, facilitates the creation of a more extensive and diverse solution set. Ultimately, we offer strategic guidance on the appropriate applications of these optimization techniques.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct agent types, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex version of the problem incorporates additive functions as the basis for agent preference lists. Although certain problem variants have established determinative matching algorithms, the additive version of Stable Roommates in three dimensions lacks a general matching algorithm, except in specific cases with particular properties. It was recently demonstrated that finding the best possible matches in the additive 3-D Stable Roommates problem involves solving a combinatorially complex optimization issue. This study presents an efficient algorithm for finding stable matchings that maximize agents' satisfaction in the additive 3-D Stable Roommates problem.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we find that two mechanisms, cone tilt and
cone variation, have distinct effects on valley Hall responses. However, when we
allow for more flexible strain variations, our results indicate that the valley Hall
effect vanishes. Moreover, a novel mechanism resulting from the curvatures of the
bands, which is enabled by strain variations, gives rise to noteworthy valley
circulation phenomena. Notably, a considerable valley Hall effect can be triggered
in curvatures with double concavity patterns. Additionally, our findings suggest
that the effective mass can be manipulated by adjusting the strain, which may be
utilized to control valley transport and related phenomena. Our research lays the
ground for the in-depth examination of electron-phonon interactions in 2D materials
under conditions of varying strain.

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To clarify this phenomenon, we investigate the stability of these space transformations. A cloud is considered to be stable if its distances remain unchanged under any general transformation. However, we demonstrate that no such general rule exists to maintain distances within a cloud, thereby proving it is inconsistent with previous assumptions. Furthermore, we define and study a specific type of stable space, called the center of its Gromov--Hausdorff class, by observing that the limits of converging clouds are also consistent with these space transformations. The class of all spaces with their distances scaled by a fixed positive factor is shown to converge uniformly to the center of their respective Gromov--Hausdorff class. Additionally, we define and study a specific metric on the Gromov--Hausdorff class by taking the infimum of the distances between its member spaces, demonstrating that this metric is complete.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a microstrip patch and an intrinsic chip beam. The combination enables both broad and wide coverage through variations in inclination angle. The antenna's wide angle of coverage is a result of its unique chip beam characteristic, which transitions from a chip beam to a microstrip patch beam as the angle increases. The merge of these two beams occurs within a relatively small angle of coverage. The microstrip patch beam dominates at lower frequencies within the specified bandwidth, while the chip beam dominates at higher frequencies. The antenna's performance was optimized using numerical simulations, which confirmed its wide angle of coverage and broad bandwidth. These results were further validated by the measurement of the microstrip patch beam and the measurement of the microstrip patch and chip beams combining at higher frequencies.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which a range of reinforcement learning strategies can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using the surface code as a model, we develop and evaluate a simplified 2D neural network decoder based on deep reinforcement learning. This approach is found to function remarkably well, extracting clear patterns from the code environment and extracting clear patterns from the code environment and extracting clear patterns from the code environment and extracting clear patterns. This approach extracts clear patterns from the code environment and extracting clear patterns. This approach proves that fault-tolerant decoding can be learned, providing new perspectives on the subject and offering hope for applying reinforcement learning in related areas of quantum computing.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by manipulating entangled quantum states to measure parameters such as the phases of waves. This paper proposes a new method, known as quantum jump metrology, to determine the relative phase between two optical cavities using a small number of photons. This method relies on an entangled state shared between three atoms and works by monitoring the quantum states of entangled photon pairs as they transition. The probability of detecting a click while analyzing the state is highly sensitive to the target phase, offering potential improvements in precision. Additionally, this method's reliance on thermal photons is fully accounted for, indicating that quantum fluctuations can reach an accuracy superior to that achieved by other methods using similar resources.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog quantum computers can efficiently simulate complex fermionic systems, which are crucial in condensed matter and materials science. By outlining a simulation protocol, we demonstrate that fermionic systems can be effectively replicated, and compute the critical correlation functions necessary for determining key properties such as phase transitions and magnetic orders. Furthermore, our simulations show that the bias towards anti-symmetry in fermionic systems can be accurately replicated, and we propose a method to determine the critical exponents for second-order phase transitions. Lastly, our study includes a detailed analysis of the resources required to perform these simulations, taking into account the inefficiencies of analog quantum computers and taking steps to minimize them, and shows that digital-analog quantum computers offer advantages in simulating fermionic systems over traditional gate-model quantum computers.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that are difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach for constructing a robust feature space that encodes relevant information from the input data and generates high-confidence outputs with uncertain inputs labeled as OoD. This space is obtained by solving a classical problem from computational geometry, resulting in a set of features that are both informative and reliable for classification purposes.

The proposed Rich Feature Construction (RFC) approach offers several advantages over existing solutions: it is straightforward to implement, can be efficiently computed even for large datasets, and is not susceptible to overfitting. Moreover, RFC is a feature-level method that is independent of the chosen model architecture. Our experiments confirm that RFC is a reliable and effective solution to the optimization-generalization problem.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our binary WMA-GA system, our new design features a binary-weighted, iterative, flip-based liquid crystal display (iFLC-SLM) that enhances structure formation precision, accommodates higher wavefront modulation requirements, and utilizes a simplified binary-weighted approach for wavefront optimization. Our system features a binary-weighted, iterative, flip-based iFLC-SLM that uses a binary-weighted approach for wavefront optimization. Our results demonstrate that this system achieves wavefront modulation with high accuracy and maintains a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) when dealing with structured illumination, even when encountering noise levels as high as 5%. Additionally, our system successfully forms intricate air-like structures inside a tissue phantom at a speed of 10 μm/s, surpassing our original binary GA system which achieved a speed of 1.4 μm/s.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is the first to explore a specific learning problem - learning an optimal treatment policy in the context of non-parametric treatment response models, under conditions of high dependence and non-identatity, utilizing data from multiple sources with known distribution shifts. The discussion highlights complexities not addressed in our original paper, such as the influence of treatment covariate distributions and non-uniform treatment shifts. Future research can be directed at addressing these issues.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across different thicknesses under various beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, subsequently yielding significant gains in detection efficiency and spatial/temporal resolution.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at the speed of milliseconds.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model. It combines the difference of two independent square-root processes, similar to Pelsser's exogenous model but employs a distinct deterministic adjustment mechanism. We derive exact analytical solutions for the probability density function and cumulative distribution function of negative interest rates. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of this new model, comparing it to Pelsser's model through Monte Carlo simulations.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the assumption that sterile neutrinos mix with light active neutrinos, which would result in prominent signals within DUNE's sensitivity. We find that DUNE has the capability to detect sterile neutrinos with masses up to approximately 1.3 GeV for certain combinations of mixing parameters. We employ a lima bean-shaped detector configuration and realistic experimental limitations, which yield results consistent with previous predictions for LHCb and NA62 experiments. Additionally, our study explores the prospects of DUNE in searching for sterile neutrinos within several distinct scenarios: the sterile neutrino as a dark matter candidate, production of sterile neutrinos through dark matter decay or particle interactions, and related parameters affecting DUNE's potential discoveries.

Meta-analyses that include multiple studies sharing common factors often employ mixed-effects models to analyze these biases.  The standard approach for such analyses is to both remove variance between studies and account for covariates that may influence results.  However, when analyzing the interdependencies between two outcomes in meta-analores, direct application of mixed effects may not always produce reliable estimates due to issues with non-stationary residuals.  In order to address this challenge, new cluster-robust variance estimators, specifically the White capture-Boverdijk type, have been proposed to deal with non-stationary residual variances in conjunction with common factors.  Through simulations, our findings suggest that these new estimators perform well in the presence of common factors, even when the number of studies is relatively small.  The proposed method has been successfully applied in a real-world analysis of psychological studies.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions using various scenarios including a particle-particle collision, a particle-wall collision with velocity normal to the wall and a particle-wall collision with varying impact angles. Our algorithm significantly reduces the number of necessary integration steps by allowing for larger collision time steps, often up to 50 times the flow time steps, with an average increase in simulation efficiency of 30%. Our method also successfully replicated the law of conservation of momentum for particle collisions, with a mean error rate less than 0.0001%.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different levels of broadening, with some aligning with and others deviating from theoretical and experimental predictions. An analysis of the dependence of broadening on the parton's initial transverse momentum reveals distinct trends in different models. These findings can be further validated by examining the parton's transverse momentum distribution as it passes through the nucleus. An initial comparison with experimental data shows a reasonable agreement in the low-Q^2 region, with room for potential improvement in the high-Q^2 region through a more intricate model that incorporates parton transverse momentum.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this paper, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over existing methods in terms of runtime overhead, with an average additional time of 1.43 microseconds to ensure crash tolerance. Our comprehensive evaluations involve a variety of algorithms and show that this method offers superior results compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the characteristic escape distances, the frequencies of stable and metastable configurations, and the distribution of lifetimes. These measures showed near-perfect agreement with the predicted theoretical values. Notably, even with a low statistical count of non-ergodic systems with equal masses (approximately 3.4%), the predicted and actual values differed minimally, and not a single measure exceeded a discrepancy of 0.04 from the theoretical statistics. When equal masses were varied, the prediction and actual values showed discrepancies of up to 2% for escape probabilities and up to 5% for lifetime distributions. The theory's performance is presented as the standard against which future theories will be judged.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The study found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than that of J/$\psi$ mesons over the entire examined momentum range.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting. By leveraging parallel calculation capabilities
on multicore systems, we enhance testing speed, enabling more extensive testing
within limited time.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets consist of asynchronous, variable-length, randomly sampled sequences which are modelled separately using Recurrent Neural Networks and combined through the alignment of hidden states, along with attention and pre-training schemes to handle differing sequence lengths. Experimental outcomes using 1023 patients' data demonstrate that the combined model outperforms EHR-only and EPA models in predicting suicidal ideation risk across multiple time points within a year.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a $\sim 1$ degree radius around Cassiopeia A with the X-ray Polarization Explorer. Utilizing IXPE's 11 observations, a combined signal was extracted within the 3-7 keV energy range, yielding a 95% confidence polarization level of $1.8 \pm 0.3$%. Assuming a 100% polarization instrument efficiency, we estimated a lower limit on the $3-4$ keV emission's polarization degree of $2.5 \pm 0.5$%. Through modeling, we attribute the observed polarization as a product of both bombshell and outer shock radiation, with a particular contribution of $\sim 30%$ from the bombshell. Our findings facilitate a greater comprehension of shock physics and nuclear radiation, thus contributing to the ongoing study of supernova remnant evolution.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior depends on the complex properties of dense matter.  In this context, a simplified description of dense matter using three symmetric effective mass nucleons* and an equal mixture of hyperons* offers a reasonable approximation, leading to a sound velocity profile that matches various compact star observations.  In this article, we will examine the properties of dense matter and their effects on compact stars, using the simplified description.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular shapes such as bubbles, droplets, and foam, significant distortions occur, even within their internal structures. Understanding the morphology of these interfaces is crucial for the study of mass transfer processes. While the distorted shapes present in such systems can easily be perceived visually, accurately characterizing their geometry in a quantitative manner proves to be a difficult task. In this research, we propose the use of skeletal representations of 3D datasets as a unified approach for characterizing the topology of interfaces with varied morphologies. Skeletalization involves identifying the critical points of an object's surface, linking them to represent the overall shape. This process is both morphology-independent and invariant to the image acquisition methodology, making skeletalization a versatile technique. Furthermore, skeletalization does not rely on ground truth data, simplifying its implementation in an automated skeletalization framework. We tested skeletalization on a variety of systems with intricate interfaces, including a creeping foam, a laminar jet of water mixed with sugar, and simulations of bubbly mixtures. In addition, we outline potential applications of skeletalization and propose modifications to further enhance its performance.
